doc.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000

title: Playing 'Mr. Andrew J. Caddick' and its simplicity
summary: They listen to a new tune written for his manager, with Cary's guitar voicings.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: A tune on that?
Just to play a little bit.
You want to play one of mine?
Yeah, I’d love to.
What kind of groove do you want?
I want something pretty funky.
Something pretty funky? Did we do anything funky on there? It’s not funky but it’s really charming. It’s called “Mr. Andrew J. Caddick.” I don’t know what track that is.
I’ll have to look in there I think.
Yeah, you’ve got your glasses. I wrote this for my manager who has been with me for the last, over ten years, young dude.
There it is.
Andrew Caddick.
Okay.
[audio interlude]
I love that bass sound. It’s beautiful.
It’s just bass and guitar and drums.
[audio interlude]
And it’s got that little flow man, it swings.

Beautiful. Can you recall when you first brought this to the group, how much describing — for instance, that guitar thing. Did you describe to your guitar player I want something kind of ethereal or did you let them try things and guide them?
No not really, I didn’t have to tell Cary what to do. No.
That’s why you have him, right?

Exactly. I just wrote the melody and that was all, just blow. And his voicing of his chords, that’s his, that’s Cary’s thing. It’s a complete departure from everything else on the album, but it’s [scats] a simple little melody.
That’s nice.

See you can’t — there’s no substitute for simplicity and continuity. It’s just like patience and fortitude, really. But simplicity and continuity, these are the things that are very effective. These are the things that are haunting, these are the things that you remember, your brain retains.
Yes. It’s singable. It’s lovely. Well that’s great.
